query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a uniform thin hafnium (Hf) coating to a refractory high‐entropy alloy will improve its high‐temperature oxidation resistance by forming a dense, stable HfO2 scale that protects the underlying material.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., a V–Zr–Hf–Nb–Ta alloy) in its as‐fabricated state without any dedicated oxidation-resistant surface treatment.
generation.intervention: Deposition of a thin, uniform Hf coating (e.g., via physical vapor deposition) on the alloy’s surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure at elevated temperatures (about 1000–1100 °C) in an oxygen-rich atmosphere (air) for long durations (50–200 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent HfO2 layer on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: During high‐temperature exposure, the applied Hf coating preferentially oxidizes to form a protective HfO2 film. This oxide is thermodynamically stable with low oxygen permeability, thereby inhibiting further oxygen diffusion into the underlying alloy and reducing subsequent oxidation and degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated samples, the Hf-coated alloy will show significantly lower mass gain (indicative of reduced oxide formation), fewer surface defects (e.g., less spallation or pulverization), and better retention of mechanical properties after high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory high‐entropy alloys that typically develop more severe oxide scales and higher weight gain under the same high-temperature oxidation conditions.
generation.boundary: The benefit is expected to be most pronounced under high-temperature (≥1000 °C) oxidation conditions in air; performance under reduced oxygen pressures or lower temperatures may not be similarly enhanced, and the optimal coating thickness and long-term cyclic stability require further investigation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal thickness for the Hf coating and its durability under thermal cycling remain to be quantified. Additionally, the effects of possible interdiffusion between the coating and alloy at extreme temperatures are not fully resolved.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical refractory HEA samples. Deposit a thin Hf coating (of controlled thickness) on one set while leaving the other set untreated. Subject both sets to an oxidation test at 1050 °C in static air for 100 hours. During and after exposure, assess mass gain, oxide layer morphology (by SEM and XRD), and mechanical properties (e.g., hardness) of the samples.
measurements: Microstructure and continuity of the surface oxide (via SEM/XRD)
Retention of hardness or other mechanical properties
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in mass gain, form a continuous protective HfO2 layer, and maintain superior mechanical properties relative to the untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-temperature oxidation-resistant VZrHfNbTa refractory HEA-based Hf-coated composites are prepared by the combined process. It has a coating thickness of 120 μm. Vanadium, niobium, tantalum and hafnium elements in the base alloy have obvious boundaries with the hafnium coating, and the zirconium element undergoes diffusion and migration in the coating with a diffusive distance of about 60 μm. High-temperature oxidation tests show that the weight gain per unit area of the coated sample is much less than that of the uncoated sample. Dents and pulverization on the surface of the alloy after oxidation of the uncoated specimen, oxidation, and sintering on the surface of the coated specimen result in the formation of a dense HfO2 protective layer. The coating can effectively improve the oxidation resistance of the material in extreme environments and prevent the surface from chalking, thus extending the material’s service life and broadening the application.
